title: Ruth
versionTitle: Rut; Based on Malbim. Trans. M Atlas, 2026
text: Once upon a time, when Israel was so lawless that the commonfolk judged their judges rather than vice versa, God punished them, and a famine befell the land. Concerned that the hungry and unruly masses would sack his property, one esteemed nobleman left Bethlehem in Judah to dwell temporarily in the fields of Mo'av. He went with his wife and two sons who complied with his wishes and joined him.

This renowned gentleman was named Elimelech, his wife was named Na'omi, and his two sons were named Machlon and Kilyon. They were members of the renowned and honorable Efrat dynasty of Bethlehem, Judah. After travelling east, they came to the fields of Mo'av, where, contrary to plan, they established themselves with permanent lodgings.

God was very displeased with Elimelech's behaviour. Therefore, providence had him lose all his money and status. Ultimately, Elimelech died a providential and untimely death, by which point he was simply known to all as the husband of Na'omi. She and her two sons survived him.

But the two sons did not heed the providential message. They even married Moabite women who took their fancy. The first was named Orpah, and the second—who so happened to be a woman of outstanding character—was named Rut. They were settled there for about ten years.
God was displeased with their behaviour too. Therefore, Machlon and Kilyon too died providential and untimely deaths. The woman Na'omi, however, survived her two sons and husband.

Concerned that their home was cursed, Na'omi and her daughters-in-law packed up and left their home, intent on relocation. Na'omi decided the time was right to return to Bethlehem for she had received message that YHWH, once more, viewed His people favourably, and had granted them bread. She thus commenced her return journey westwards, away from the fields of Mo'av.

She departed the place where she had established herself, along with her two daughters-in-law. Once they took to the road, the daughters-in-law decided to accompany Na'omi to the Land of Judah. Thus, they all travelled the westward road back to the land of Judah.

Assuming that they were kindly escorting her to the border so that she need not travel alone, Na'omi said to her two daughters-in-law: "You need not accompany me! You may leave me! You may each return to your mother's home! May YHWH act kindly towards you, just as you acted so kindly towards the dead and myself."
Moreover, may YHWH grant you fine new husbands, that each of you may find peace as a wife in her husband's home. With that, she kissed them goodbye, and they wailed and wept together.

But Na'omi had misunderstood her daughter-in-laws' intentions in accompanying her. They clarified and said to her: "No! You misunderstood! We are travelling with you because we intend to return to your people with you!"

Na'omi did not consider this a wise idea. So she said to them: "You must return, my daughters! Why do you wish to travel with me! Do you not realize that no Judean will offer their sons in marriage to Moabite widow-converts? Are you fantasizing that I conceal more boys in my innards who might be husbands for you?"

"No, you must return, my daughters! For I have no boys hiding in my abdomen! And obviously I cannot bear any more sons whom you could marry when they come of age! For I am too old to beget offspring with a man! Moreover, even if I said to myself that there is hope for me to bear a child and I was with a man this very night, and I even bore a child"

Would you rest all your hopes on them? Can you be so confident that they will make it to marriageable age? Even if you consider this a likely outcome, ought you remain alone, deprived of husband, in order to marry them? For, by the time they come of age, would you be able to engage in a meaningful, let alone a childbearing, relationship with them!? Mourn, my daughters! Know that my lot is more bitter than yours, for the striking hand of YHWH has thoroughly spent itself on me.

Recognizing the painful choice they faced, they again wailed and wept together. Orpah decided that she was not willing to sacrifice marriage prospects for Judah. She kissed her mother-in-law goodbye and headed off home, while Rut, who was not willing to sacrifice Judah and Judaism for marriage prospects, remained committed to her.
Na'omi said to her: "Look, your sister-in-law has returned home; ostensibly to her native people but, in reality, also to her former gods! Follow your sister-in-law's lead and return too!"

But Rut replied: "Please do not expect concessions from me when you encourage me to leave you personally, all the more so to no longer follow you to Judah and Judaism. Please do not assault my spirituality. For I am ideologically committed to Judaism. I wish to go to where you are going, because the land of Israel is as meaningful to me as it is to you! I do not seek worldly comforts; where you casually rest as you work towards the afterlife, I shall casually rest. Your people is as much mine as it yours; Your God is as much mine as it is yours."

I seek the same death and afterlife prospects that you do, and I intend to be buried there—in the holy soil of Judah from where the dead will resurrect. May YHWH strike me thus once more, may He increase the severity of His blows if I fail to follow through! For I realize that if I fail to fully embrace Judaism, my earthly life may be as tolerable as yours, but at death an enormous gulf shall separate my destiny from yours.
Na'omi then saw that Rut was adamant about accompanying her, and so she refrained from speaking further to her about this matter.

Thus the two of them walked side-by-side until they arrived in Bethlehem. When they arrived in Bethlehem, the entire town was aghast at them, exclaiming: "Is this Na'omi? Is this all that remains of Elimelech's wealth and dynasty?"

Na'omi solemnly replied to them: "You need not refer to me as the Na'omi you remember to contextualize my predicament, for I am not merely impoverished relative to the wealthy Na'omi I once was. You can refer to me as the objectively 'embittered one' for Shaddai has made my lot extremely bitter."

"In fact, YHWH providentially had me depart fullhanded and return emptyhanded! It seems my former wealth was a scaffold He had me climb to endure a more painful fall! If so, why do you refer to me as the Na'omi you remember, as though that were my baseline? It was merely YHWH cautioning me, and ultimately Shaddai's method for harming me."

Na'omi asserted her ownership rights to her husband's estate, and Rut asserted her rights to a pay-out from the estate by virtue of her marriage contract to Machlon, Elimelech's deceased heir. Thus, Na'omi and Rut the Moabite—who had returned from the fields of Mo'av and was thus entitled to assert her financial rights—completed their return to their ancestral homelands. Even though their own lands' produce could sustain them the following year, they were currently destitute for they arrived in Bethlehem at the onset of the barley harvest, with their estate utterly overgrown and uncultivated.

There was a man of valor and virtue named Bo'az, who hailed from the family of Elimelech. He was well acquainted with, and fond of, Na'omi and her former husband. He was well to do and possessed the financial means to support Na'omi and Rut until their financial situation improved. However, rather than further humiliate herself by begging relatives such as Bo'az for charity, Na'omi opted to collect the agricultural gifts bequeathed to the poor by Torah law. Yet, this too was disgraceful for her.

Rut, who was unknown to the locals due her Moabite roots, correctly read her mother-in-law's thoughts and said to Na'omi: "Fear not! I shall go to the fields and collect the agricultural gifts for it is less debasing for me, a mere stranger. I shall stay safe: I shall go only to the fields but not to the orchards where one can fall off the trees; I shall only collect fallen sheaves but not the less tedious pe'ah (the field's perimeter left for the poor to harvest) where desperate paupers may resort to jostling and violence; I shall only follow a harvester who looks at me favorably and indicates that I am welcome in his field." Relieved and grateful, Na'omi replied, "Yes, my daughter, go!"

She set off and rapidly arrived at a field. True to her word, she did not busy herself with the pe'ah. Rather, at once, she followed the harvesters up and down the field and collected the sheaves that fell as they harvested. With the other poor engaged with the pe'ah, this provided her with a calm and safe environment to go about her business. How providential that her destiny brought her to the field lot belonging to the aforementioned Bo'az of Elimelech's family!

Behold! Bo'az uncharacteristically and providentially arrived that very afternoon from the residential area of Bethlehem. He addressed the harvesters with the new customary greeting: "May YHWH be with you", to which they replied, "May YHWH bless you too".

Surprised to see Rut sitting with the farmhands in their respite hut, especially seeing that she was the sole pauper in the field, and she had amassed several large heaps of grain, Bo'az incorrectly surmised that she was in cahoots with one of the farmhands who had driven away the other paupers to give her exclusive rights to the fallen sheaves. He therefore said to the youth who managed the harvesters: With which one of you is this young woman associated?

The youth who managed the harvesters respectfully explained to Bo'az that he had erred. He then voluntarily added his personal impressions of Rut. He said: "None of us are associated with her for she is a young Moabite woman. But, we understand that she is entitled to the gifts for the poor, for she returned from the fields of Mo'av with Na'omi and converted to Judaism."

"She seems to have said to herself, 'I shall ignore the pe'ah. I shall be the first to follow the harvesters. I shall gather the fallen sheaves and compile them into little heaps.' She has been on her feet from the moment she arrived this morning until now—she has only just retreated to the respite hut for a short rest. It is therefore unsurprising that she has amassed so much grain."

Bo'az, taking kindly to Rut, turned to her and said: "Surely you heard, my daughter, how positively the manager speaks of you! Please, for your own good, do not go to gather in someone else's field; do not even transfer from this field to another of my fields. For here you will be treated well. Associate yourself with my female farmhands!"

"Focus your eyes on the field in which my female farmhands harvest and follow them. Fear not, my male farmhands shall still act kindly towards you even if you keep your distance from them, for I have instructed them not to lay a finger on you. Moreover, if you are thirsty, I grant you permission to go to their vessels and drink of the high-quality waters that the male farmhands have drawn for themselves."

Rut, overwhelmed by his kindness, lowered her face and prostrated herself on the ground before him. She then said to him, "Why do I find favor in your eyes? Why do you act as though you are acquainted with me, for I am a foreigner!?"

Bo'az replied and said to her, "But I do know of you and your family and care about them. Moreover, I am deeply impressed by you. I was informed of all the loving-kindness you have done for your mother-in-law, notwithstanding the death of your husband. This is highly unusual and testifies to your sterling character! Moreover, you left your father and mother and the land of your birth and travelled to join a nation that you had never previously encountered—not yesterday nor the day before! This testifies to your ideological resoluteness!"

"May YHWH recompense you for your charitable work with your mother-in-law! May YHWH the providential God of Israel make your reward complete and never-ending for coming to seek refuge beneath His wings by converting to Judaism!"

Grateful and empowered by his kind words, Rut replied, "May I continue to find favour in your eyes, my master. For your kind words and actions have comforted me for the first time since my husband's passing; I now know that a man is looking out for me and I shall not starve. Moreover, I felt that you spoke empathetically to me as though I was one of your household maids whom you had personally converted to Judaism. I am humbled, for I do not see myself ever being as worthy as one of your maids."

The arrival of lunchtime interrupted their impassioned conversation. As the food was served, Bo'az invited Rut to join them for lunch. He said to her, "Do come and sit here, next to me. Here, this loaf of bread is just for you! Please eat from it with us! Dip your slices in the vinegar!" However, while Rut gratefully joined them, she sat with the harvesters rather than at the table head. After the bread course was complete, Bo'az even passed her roasted kernels for dessert. Thus she ate her fill; she was satisfied and even had food to spare.

At once, she got to her feet and returned to the field to continue her collection, while the men remained to recite the grace after meals in unison. Once she had left, Bo'az—all the more impressed by Rut took it upon himself to ease Rut's condition: He therefore instructed his male farmhands as follows, "She may even gather between the stacked sheaves, and you may not humiliate her. Do not subject her to interrogation, for you need not suspect her of robbery!"

"Moreover, deliberately drop some bundled sheaves in her path so she can gather them, but first declare them ownerless (hefker) to avoid halakhic issues pertaining to the priestly gifts and tithes. Under all circumstances, do not confront her!"

But Rut was content to gather within the open field which she did until the evening. She did not approach the stacked sheaves and knew nothing of the bundles that had been deliberately dropped for her. Despite this, her diligence and endurance resulted in a successful day's collection. As evening approached, she beat the grain that she had gathered to remove the grain kernels from the straw, and discovered that she had amassed an ephah of barley—the precise amount predicted by the Sages for a day's collection in a large field that yielded a healthy crop (see Talmud Yerushalmi, pe'ah 5:1).

Rid of the straw, she wrapped the grains into a kerchief and carried them and returned to the town. Her mother-in-law stared in disbelief when she saw how much she had gathered! Rut unpacked her kerchief and offered her the barley, as well as the leftover bread from her filling lunch.

Her awestruck mother-in-law looked up and said to her, "Where did you gather fallen grains today that you managed to amass so much? And where did you find work today that you were offered bread for lunch? Evidently somebody took a liking to you; may he be blessed!" Then Rut told her mother-in-law all about her interactions with her benefactor; how he felt indebted to her for the past kindnesses she had performed for Na'omi, his relative. She concluded and said, "The name of the man with whom I interacted today is Bo'az".

When Na'omi heard that her benefactor was none other than Bo'az—the very man whom she knew would help them but whom she had been too ashamed to call, she was touched by YHWH's wonderful providence. Na'omi exclaimed, "May he be blessed to YHWH, for he has not withheld kindness from his living—us—and dead relatives—our deceased husbands". Na'omi then explained to her, "I am delighted that this man has taken a liking to you. For he is a relative of ours; he is tasked with redeeming our family heritage. I suspect he will gladly take you as his wife, and together you shall perpetuate the legacy of the dead!"

Rut, whose Mo'abite roots showed in her subtle misunderstandings, replied, "Yes indeed! I am convinced that he will look out for us financially. He even said to me, 'You may stay close to my male farmhands until they finish my entire harvest'." Rut's recollection indicated that she had misunderstood Bo'az's statement, "Associate yourself with my female farmhands!" She thought he was offering their female friendship when in fact he was requesting that she disassociate herself from his male farmhands. Likewise, Na'omi's allusion to marriage and yibum went over her head, for her reply focused solely on their improved financial situation.

So Na'omi explained to Rut Bo'az's likely intention. She said to Rut her daughter-in-law, "It is worthwhile, my daughter, to go out to the fields with his female farmhands, rather than risk being assaulted in other more remote fields by male farmhands who interpret your friendliness as suggestive."

Heeding the advice, she associated herself with the female farmhands working for Bo'az until the end of the wheat and barley harvests. Even though she forged friendships with them, she would return each evening to lodge with her dear mother-in-law of whom she was exceptionally fond.

One day, Rut's mother-in-law Na'omi said to her, "My daughter, surely it is time that I find you a peaceful abode—a husband who will care for you and improve you religiously and spiritually. I think enough time has passed since your husband's death that it is both permissible and advisable to remarry."

"Now, I would like you to pay Bo'az a night visit, but you must do so discreetly. Tonight, he will be winnowing his barley. I suggest that you attend this winnowing. Give off the impression that you have come to spend the evening supporting your girlfriends whom you have missed since the harvest completed. After all, Bo'az is our relative so no one would find it strange that you are trespassing on his farm. Likewise, everyone knows that you spent much time with his female farmhands and befriended them."

"Before you go, wash yourself and apply your cosmetic ointments and ensure you have your finest robes with you, for your objective is to spend the night with Bo'az. As the winnowing winds down, look for the opportune moment to sneak into the granary, where you must hide—unbeknownst to anyone—until all the farmhands have returned home. I suggest you don your finery and wait there until you surmise that Bo'az has finished eating and drinking."

"It will then be his bedtime. You will know exactly where he lies down for the night, because he will almost certainly make himself a haystack bed in the granary. Once in bed, approach him, uncover his feet and lie beside him. This will symbolize that he must choose between having you at his side as a marital partner (through yibum—levirate marriage) or becoming a shoeless home (Devarim 25:10). He will understand the symbolic message and instruct you what to do next. He may agree to marry you himself, or he may direct you to another relative with even closer familial ties.
After listening carefully to Na'omi's plan, Rut replied to her, "I shall do whatever you tell me, both now and after I receive instruction from Bo'az, for I value your counsel."

And so she surreptitiously observed the winnowing before excusing herself. She stealthily slipped into the granary, whereupon she followed all her mother-in-law's instructions. She dressed up in her finery, applied her remaining make-up and ointments, and lay in wait

In the meanwhile, Bo'az ate and drank to his heart's content. Then, just as Na'omi had predicted, he entered the granary to lie on a bed of hay at the edge of the haystack. Rut, as still and silent as possible in her hidden corner, waited patiently until he drifted asleep. Then, she emerged from her hiding place and furtively approached him. She uncovered his feet and lay down to sleep beside him.

She did this so gently and quietly that Bo'az did not immediately stir. It was only sometime later, in the middle of the night, that and sensed her presence. The man was gripped by panic and thrashed about, but when Rut spoke softly to him1[1] I primarily follow Ibn Ezra here (see also Sforno). Malbim does not weigh in on this pasuk., he realized that it was a woman lying at his feet.

Unable to make out who she was, he said to her, "Who are you?" She replied, "I am Rut your maid. I have come to lie with you dutifully rather than promiscuously. Please spread your wings over your maid as does a mating bird, for you are tasked with redeeming our family heritage!"

Bo'az, regaining his composure, and once more deeply impressed by Rut's incredible commitment to his family, said to her, "May you be blessed by YHWH, my daughter! Your present kindness—to pursue a levirate marriage that will perpetuate the legacy of your deceased husband—is greater than your former kindness—when you first took his hand in marriage! For now, despite being young and beautiful, you have taken upon yourself not to pursue a relationship with a young man! I have no doubt that should you so wish, you would find love—not only from a poor man, but even from a rich man!"

"Now, my daughter, fear not that I seek to extract myself with excuses! I shall do for you exactly as you say—I promise to spread my wings over you. Likewise, fear not that the townspeople will protest my marriage to a lowly Moabite convert, for all who preside over the court at the community's gate know that you are a woman of outstanding virtue."

"However, I am unable to offer myself to you tonight, for although I am indeed tasked with redeeming our family heritage, there is another fellow—named Tov—who likewise has this duty, and is a closer relative than me."

"I suggest that you stay for the night here, and tomorrow morning I shall present the situation to Tov. If Tov decides to redeem you, then he shall be the redeemer. But if he does not wish to redeem you, I swear by the vital existence of YHWH that I shall redeem you!" Upon hearing that Bo'az did not intend to lie with her that night, and perhaps never at all should Tov accept his offer, Rut felt decidedly uncomfortable about the prospect of spending the rest of the night alone with Bo'az, all made up, at his feet. She made as if to leave, but Bo'az would not hear of it; "Please, lie here until the morning. I have no doubt that I can control myself."

And so she lay at his feet until the morning was set to break whereupon she swiftly arose before it became light enough that a person could recognize another. But as she prepared to slip away, she was spotted by an attendant of Bo'az. Bo'az sternly instructed him, "It may not be known that the woman who visited the winnowing entered the granary at its conclusion rather than heading home."

Bo'az then said to Rut, "Please pass me the shawl wrapped about you and hold onto it." She did as she was told and held onto her shawl, while he measured out a "sixer" of barley—likely one sixth of the se'ah measure—and laid it upon the shawl. This was the precise amount for breakfast for two (based on Mishna, pe'ah 8:7); one serving for Rut and one serving for Na'omi. In so doing, he demonstrated his certainty that Rut would be spending the evening meal in the company of her new husband, be he Tov or himself. He then walked alongside her back to the town.

They walked swiftly, and as such Rut entered her mother-in-law's home before it was properly light. Not recognizing her, she said, "Who are you, my daughter?" Rut then related to her all that man had done for her and promised to her.
She then said, "Look, he presented me with this sixer of barley, for he said to me, 'It would not be right to come back to your mother-in-law emptyhanded. I shall provide you both with breakfast'."

Na'omi, grasping the symbolic significance of the sixer, was delighted. She said to Rut, "Rest, my daughter, until you are informed how things pan out in the court. For I am convinced that the man—Bo'az—shall not be quieted until he has settled the matter! Today!"

Meanwhile, Bo'az made his way up to the court that was situated at the town gate, where he seated himself. He was about to send a formal summons to Tov, the redeemer, to present himself before the court, when behold none other than the redeemer of whom Bo'az had spoken passed right by! Bo'az called out to him, "Kindly step aside and be seated here, Determined One Entangled One. You are entangled in a family affair, and a legal determination is necessary." He stepped aside and was seated.

He then selected ten of the city elders and said to them too, "Please be seated here". They took their seats. He required at least three judges to preside over the legal proceedings, and a congregation of at least ten to attend the ensuing marriage ceremony, in whose presence the special marital blessings could be recited. Proceedings began with a theoretical halachic debate: Is it permitted for a Jewish born male to marry a Moabite born female convert? For although it is prohibited to marry a Moabite convert (Deut. 23:4), perhaps it only applies to male converts? Though this was a controversial matter, Bo'az settled it when he informed the assembled that his schooling had acquainted him with an age-old tradition permitting female Moabite converts. Thus the first issue was resolved; Rut, despite her Moabite roots, was marriageable.

He then turned to Tov, the relative tasked with redeeming his family heritage, and said to him, "Na'omi who has returned of late from the fields of Mo'av has put up for sale the portion of the field that belonged to our brother Elimelech."

"So I said to her, 'I shall reveal this to the ears of Tov—that is, to you, for hopefully he will purchase it and keep these ancestral lands within our family. I shall say to him: Purchase it in the presence of the assembled, in the presence of the elders of my people! If you are inclined to redeem it, that is, to purchase it yourself and thereby spare it from foreign ownership, please redeem it! And should he refuse to redeem it'... So, Tov, to cut a long story short, please tell me your decision—for there are none besides you with first redemption rights, and I am next in line after you." To which Tov replied, "I shall gladly redeem it".

Bo'az then said, "But do realize that the land is co-owned by Na'omi and Rut the Mo'abite. Thus, on the same day you acquire the deeds to the field from Na'omi's hand, I believe it is incumbent on you to acquire it from Rut the Mo'abite too—by taking as your wife she who was once married to the field's deceased heir. And, do realize that you must so in order to perpetuate the legacy of the dead within his former estate."

Realizing that strings were attached, Tov—the redeemer—became disinterested. He said to Bo'az, :"Oh, so I am unable to redeem the field and put it in my own name! If so, I am concerned that this could harm my estate planning. I would rather you redeem whatever I am entitled to redeem, for I am unable to do so."

In bygone times, the Israelite custom for redeeming ancestral lands, or for bartering commodities—that is, to legally validate all proceedings, was: One party would remove their shoe and present it to the other party. And this ancient method was now adopted by Bo'az to certify his purchase amongst the Israelites. The legal calculations for his choosing this method are complex; suffice it to say that the standard practice at that time—smashing a barrel of treats before children to create a cheerful commotion—was inappropriate given the yibum and Mo'abite contexts.
The redeemer, Tov, then said to Bo'az, "Go ahead and acquire for yourself my right to purchase from me." And he slipped off his shoe.

Sometime thereafter, but still on that same day, once Bo'az had finalized his payment plans, drawn up contracts, and informed Rut of his wish to marry her, Bo'az returned to the court with his bride at his side, and Na'omi in tow. He said to the town elders and all the assembled crowd, "Today I appoint you as witnesses that I have purchased from the hand of Na'omi all that once belonged to Elimelech, and subsequently to his sons and heirs, Machlon and Kilyon."

Moreover, I have taken for myself, as my wife, Rut the Moabite, formerly the wife of Machlon, with the stated intention of perpetuating the legacy of the dead within his former estate, so that the legacy of the dead shall not be erased from his brethren nor from these gates—those of his former place of residence. Behold, you are witnesses today!"

Whereupon all the crowd who had assembled at the gates as well as the elders exclaimed, "We are witnesses!" They then blessed the couple, "May YHWH bring about that this woman who now enters your home become like our matriarchs Rachel and Leah, both of whom, despite their idolatrous upbringings, became worthy of building the Israelite establishment in the company of their righteous husbands. May you too bear progeny fit to lead our nation! May you flourish in all regards and become the pride of the Efrat dynasty, and through your achievements bring fame to our hometown Bethlehem!"

"May your home become associated with and as noble as the House of Peretz, who—although born to Yehuda by Tamar in murky yibum circumstances—grew into the grand House of Yehuda. May all this come about through the offspring that YHWH shall grant you with this young woman!"

Bo'az proceeded to take Rut as his wife by offering her a token sum of money or a contract. She became his wife and he came intimately to her. YHWH gifted her with a providential pregnancy for her former more youthful husband had not managed to impregnate her, and she gave birth to a son.

Upon hearing the good news, the womenfolk congratulated Na'omi and said to her, "Blessed is YHWH for today it is evident that He did not scheme to deprive you of a redeemer! Although He had you lose your husband and sons, He has today ensured that their legacy continue through the son levirately born to Rut! Moreover, he will undoubtedly enjoy a rosy future and become famous amongst Israel!"

He shall reincarnate Machlon's soul for you, and he shall provide for you in your old age, for he was born to your daughter-in-law who loves you dearly, such that she is better to you than seven sons!
Inspired by her women friends, Na'omi loved the baby as if her was her own. She would take the baby and cradle him in her bosom; she became his nanny.

Thus, the neighbors nicknamed him "Ben Na'omi" as if to say, "This baby was born to Na'omi". They also named him Oved as if to pray, "May this baby be of outstanding service to God". He would become the father of Yishai, the father of King David.
And so Bo'az and Rut merited to perpetuate the generations of the noble—and ultimately royal—House of Peretz: Peretz gave birth to Chetzron.
Chetzron gave birth to Ram; Ram gave birth to Aminandav.
Aminadav gave birth to Nachshon; Nachshon gave birth to Salmah.
Salmah gave birth to Bo'az; Bo'az gave birth to Oved.
Oved gave birth to Yishai, and Yishai gave birth to David.
